title: Wheels and flags
hookLine: prayer wheels turned by hand, prayer flags in the wind: the mantra carried by movement
tomorrow: Four thoughts that turn the mind
last: CHENREZIG — THE JEWEL IN THE LOTUS.

lines: THE FLAG AND THE WIND, AGAIN.
THOUSANDS OF FLAGS ON A PASS.
cards: A few weeks ago you met a koan: two monks arguing over a flag in the wind. Is the flag moving, or the wind?
Today there are thousands of flags, strung across mountain passes, from rooftops, over bridges, snapping in color against the sky.

Beside the monastery walls stand rows of painted drums on spindles, and pilgrims walk past, spinning each one with the right hand. Nobody's reading anything. And yet, Tibetans say, the words are being said.

teach.h: A SCROLL ROLLED INSIDE A DRUM.
teach.b: Start with the wheel. Tibetans call it a mani wheel, after yesterday's mantra. Inside the drum is a long, tightly rolled scroll printed with om mani padme hum, over and over.

Turn it once, clockwise, and tradition counts it as saying every mantra inside. Some wheels are small, held in the hand, with a weight on a chain to keep them spinning. Some are giant, in their own little houses.
Some sit in streams so the water turns them day and night, and some spin in the rising heat of a lamp. Now the flags.
A traditional set has five colors in a fixed order: blue, white, red, green, yellow, often linked to sky, wind, fire, water and earth.

teach.h: FIVE COLORS AND THE WIND HORSE.
teach.b: Each is printed with mantras and prayers, and many carry a horse with a jewel on its back: the lungta, the wind horse. The flags aren't hung to bless the person who hung them.
They're hung high so the wind carries the blessing outward, to every being it touches.

teach.h: MEANT TO FADE, MEANT FOR ALL.
teach.b: And they're meant to fade. Sun and wind wear the print away, and in a sense that's the mantra going out into the world.
New flags are often hung at the Tibetan New Year, and old ones are retired with respect, never tossed on the ground. Does a spinning drum really count? Tibetans answer in different ways.
For some, the turning is enough. Some teachers add that it means most when the mind turns with it, toward others. Either way, the teaching rides on movement: hands, water, fire, air.

how: Tibetan Buddhists spin hand-held and monastery prayer wheels clockwise, often while walking around a temple, and hang five-colored prayer flags on passes and rooftops, often renewing them at the Tibetan New Year and retiring faded ones respectfully.

o: the wooden drum that holds a prayer scroll
the wind horse printed on prayer flags
a pony ridden on Tibetan pilgrimages

games.q: match the pieces of wheels and flags.

s: prayer flags send blessings only to the person who hangs them
they're hung so the wind carries the blessing to every being it touches.
some prayer wheels are turned by streams or by a lamp's heat
hands, water, fire and air all keep the mantra moving.
faded flags are a sign of failure
fading is expected; the print wearing into the wind is part of the idea.

games.q: the prayer flags on your roof have faded almost white after a year of sun and wind. what's the custom?
o: hang new ones and retire the old with respect.
games.why: new flags are often hung at the Tibetan New Year; old ones are never tossed on the ground, and many people burn them respectfully.

practice: Turn something slowly, a cup in your hands or just your hand drawing a clockwise circle in the air, and with each turn send a small wish outward, to no one in particular: may someone somewhere be at ease.
After three or four turns, set it down, rest your hands, and feel the stillness after the movement. Then let the breath do the turning.

wordCard.voice: Lungta. The wind horse printed on Tibetan prayer flags, carrying blessings outward on the wind to every being they touch.

orig.note: Tibetan rlung rta: rlung (wind) + rta (horse), the wind horse printed on prayer flags.

carryVoice: Your line: the wind carries it. A blessing that's sent, not kept. See you tomorrow.
